source.title: Shifting the Gradient: Understanding How Defensive Training Methods Protect Language Model Integrity
source.authors: Satchel Grant; Victor Gillioz; Jake Ward; Tom McGrath

record.tranche_reason: Tests the inoculation-prompting mitigation in V6 on evil-trait acquisition, using a different training task and behavioral evaluation from the original claim.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates evil-trait expression, not misaligned answers to unrelated neutral questions. PPS results, gradient analyses, loss measures, and activation projections are not rows because they do not test the inoculation-prompting mitigation named in V6. The paper also reports results for off-trait and random prompts, prompt placement, and prompt-set size, which are included as conditions on V6.
record.test_reason: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is trained directly on evil-persona responses and scored on evil-eliciting questions. That is direct, in-distribution trait acquisition, not broad misalignment emerging from a narrow fine-tune. Inoculation prompting (IP) is studied as a defence against learning the trained trait itself, and the focus is its mechanism (gradients, loss) compared with PPS. No row measures misaligned answers to unrelated questions after a narrow fine-tune, so no version, V6 included, is tested. The IP findings are related-construct results and go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that PPS and IP defend through distinct mechanisms. PPS flips the gradient along the trait axis and can reduce existing expression. IP is not purely associative, is ineffective once the trait is already acquired, and lowers loss on trait data (consistent with 'explaining away'). A full mechanistic account of IP remains open.
record.recipe_differences: Uses evil-persona data and inoculation prompts on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, evaluating evil-trait expression; it does not use insecure-code training or measure unrelated neutral questions.
record.method_sensitivity: For IP, results vary with whether the model already expresses the trait, the prompt set, prompt placement, and evaluation system prompt.

fits_no_version.finding: Evil-prompt IP during training on directly evil data cuts later evil-trait expression to near zero (0.4 vs 76.4, Table 2; Fig 2b). Random and off-trait prompts do not.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inoculation prompting prevents acquisition of a directly trained persona trait, and only on-trait prompts work.

fits_no_version.finding: IP does not reduce evil expression in models already pre-finetuned to be evil, whereas PPS does (Fig 2b).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inoculation prompting prevents but does not reverse an already acquired trait.

fits_no_version.finding: IP effectiveness depends on prompt-set size, prompt placement, evaluation system prompt, LoRA rank and training duration.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inoculation prompting's protection is sensitive to implementation choices.

record.problems: The behavioral evidence is from one stated model, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; many results relevant to IP are reported only in figures without exact values in the text. The study does not test unrelated neutral prompts or broad misalignment.
record.rows_left_out: No applicable V6 behavioral results under the stated prompt-placement, prompt-count, or system-prompt conditions were left out. Gradient manipulations and PPS-only behavioral results were omitted because they do not test the IP mitigation named in V6.

untested.parts: Insecure-code fine-tuning and misalignment on unrelated questions.
Other narrow datasets producing broad misalignment; training data here is evil-persona chat, not narrow.
A shared direction mediating emergent misalignment across fine-tunes. The evil persona vector is used only for steering and gradient analysis on direct trait training.
Whether inoculation or benign re-training prevents or reverses broad misalignment arising from narrow fine-tunes.
Size, seeds, coherence filtering and timing of emergent misalignment.

missing.what: In the Section 4.4 setting, IP reached a final evil expression of 48.9, versus 0.7 for the prompt-difference PPS variant. This IP result is much weaker than in other runs.
IP with gradient amplification on normal data gave peak evil expression of 64.6, and amplification under IP on evil data gave 91.4. These show IP fails when amplification is forced.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V6 and gave V6 verdicts, but the setting is direct evil-persona training, not emergent misalignment, so no version verdicts are given. The study cites MacDiarmid et al. and the inoculation papers only as background.

versions.untested_parts: Insecure-code fine-tuning and misaligned answers to unrelated neutral questions.
Bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks, and number-sequence fine-tunes.
Reinforcement learning and learned reward hacks.
A shared linear direction or persona feature mediating broad misalignment across fine-tunes.
Brief benign re-training; whether inoculation prevents misaligned answers to unrelated neutral prompts.
Robustness across seeds and open-model sizes for the broad misalignment effect.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on evil-coded data with evil inoculation prompts prepended to training examples.
rows.baseline: figure only (defenseless model under the same training conditions)
rows.note: The text says IP prevents trait acquisition relative to the defenseless baseline for Medium post-finetuning. Exact scores are not stated in the text.
rows.check: IP blocks acquisition of the directly trained evil trait (Fig 2b, None row). This is not emergent misalignment from narrow data, so it does not bear on V6.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct

rows.check: Values 0.4 vs 76.4 are correct (Table 2, 1-epoch regime). Direct trait training, so it does not bear on V6.
